<reason>PRO built a clean, consistent path: the legal system already imposes reversible, pre-conviction burdens on predictions (psychiatric holds, ex parte protective orders, pretrial detention, warrants), and firearm removal is the least intrusive and most targeted of these. PRO tested CON's "existing tools" against a concrete case (the brother threatening suicide tonight) and showed each tool either fails or leaves the gun in the house. CON argued honestly and coherently for a "predicate" line (past act or clinical finding), and its points about home searches, seizure-before-hearing, and lingering records were real. But CON's pressure-question answers exposed the weakness PRO targeted: CON's alternative is to seize the whole person and then "more treatment or extended commitment," while never touching the object—and CON's claim that release from a hold shows the person was not dangerous enough to disarm is a strained inference PRO easily turned. PRO parried CON's "what restores the right" question by noting detention leaves no self-defense at all plus a psychiatric record. CON's closing largely repeated the predicate line without answering the "more intrusive and less effective" charge. PRO's execution was marred by clipping in three speeches, which tempers the margin, but the surviving text carried the decisive weighing. Both sides used ordinary background knowledge without fake precision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 and follow-through in R2/closing: forcing CON to admit it prefers confining the whole person over holding the rifle, then framing CON's rule as "the state may take your body but never your cabinet," while CON's "if clinicians release him, that undercuts taking his arms" answer conceded the gun stays in the house exactly where the risk is.</best_rebuttal>
